\title{\textbf{Stages 1 and 2: the frozen models, 4B against 8B}}
\author{}
\date{2026-11-01; token-budget section added 2026-11-25}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\noindent
\emph{Superseded protocol.} These runs use the code-block replies, in which a
reply was read by its contents. That protocol was replaced by the agent loop
on 2026-11-25, and the runs under it are in
\texttt{docs/stage12\_agent\_loop.tex}. This document stays as the record of
what the frozen models did under the earlier rule.

\noindent
Stages~1 and~2 put the brief in front of a frozen language model, with no
training, and score the controller it writes exactly as training will score
it. Stage~1 gives the model one turn: the brief without the probe section,
and the controller straight away. Stage~2 gives it the two-turn protocol: an
optional probe run on a throwaway batch, whose printed output comes back to
it, then the controller. This document compares two models on the same
batches, \texttt{Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507}, the base the training stages use,
and \texttt{Qwen3-8B} in non-thinking mode, twice its size from the same
generation. Both are read against the references Stage~0 fixed on the same
held-out tasks. Section~\ref{sec:budget} repeats the 4B runs with four times
the token budget, to separate what the model writes from what the budget cuts.

\paragraph{Terms.} A \emph{sample} is one rollout on one task at the sampling
temperature. \emph{Valid} means the reply held a controller that passed
validation (a \texttt{def policy(state)} with only the allowed imports).
\emph{Success} and \emph{fast success} are the environment's own outcome and
success within $1.25\times$ the oracle's steps; \emph{normalised time} is
oracle steps over own steps, zero on failure. The \emph{ride ratio} is the
highest reported $\sigma$ of the final run divided by the batch's limit: one
is the oracle, lower is caution, above one is a shower. The \emph{probe rate}
is the share of Stage~2 samples whose first reply the runner took as probe
code rather than a controller: any first reply in which it finds no top-level
\texttt{def policy}, which includes a controller whose code does not parse
(Table~\ref{tab:first-replies}). The \emph{estimate error} is how far the number closest to the
true limit in the probe's printed output lies from it. \emph{Cut off} means
the reply opened a code block the token budget closed before it ended.
\emph{Ruined} is a shower or lost seeds; \emph{error} is a controller that
did not run, scored at the error floor.

\section{Protocol}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
  \item \textbf{Tasks.} The \SFntasks\ held-out tasks of
  \texttt{crystallizer\_eval.jsonl}, 16 per third of the limit's range, the
  same batches as Stage~0's references.
  \item \textbf{Samples.} \SFnsamples\ per task per run at temperature $0.8$,
  top-$p$ $0.95$, at most \SFmaxtokens\ new tokens per turn.
  \item \textbf{Brief.} The brief of the paper's appendix, with the two quench
  logs and the stated range of the limit; Stage~1 without the probe section.
  \item \textbf{Models.} \texttt{Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507} (instruct-only, no
  thinking mode) and \texttt{Qwen3-8B} with thinking switched off through the
  chat template's \texttt{enable\_thinking=False}, as its model card
  instructs; bf16 weights, one A30 each, no gradient updates.
  \item \textbf{Scoring.} The runner's sandbox: the probe run on the probe
  batch with the limit masked, the controller on the scoring batch,
  \texttt{score\_sample} as the trainer uses it.
  \item \textbf{References.} The cautious blind controller and the oracle of
  Stage~0, on the same tasks.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Reading}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.5em]
  \item \textbf{Both frozen models sit far below the cautious blind
  reference.} The 4B base scores $-84$ in one turn and $-66$ with the
  two-turn protocol; the 8B scores $-207$ and $-192$. The cautious blind
  controller, which never probes and never fails, scores $+38$; the oracle
  $+80$; the hand-written probe run and controller of Stage~0, $+77$. No run
  reaches fast success on more than one sample in a hundred. The headroom for
  training is the whole scale.

  \item \textbf{The 8B is worse than the 4B on every column, and the reason
  is in Table~\ref{tab:errors}:} 91 and 90 of its 192 samples never run. Its
  controllers use \texttt{L} without reading it from the state or refer to an
  \texttt{initial\_L} they never set (49 undefined names in Stage~1); they
  read \texttt{state['done']} although the brief states that \texttt{done} is
  returned by \texttt{env.step} and the flags are attributes of \texttt{env}
  (7 crashes in Stage~1, 33 in Stage~2); and in Stage~2 they call \texttt{env}
  inside the controller although the brief states the controller has no
  access to it (37 controllers contain \texttt{env.step} or
  \texttt{env.reset}, 21 crash on it). In non-thinking mode the 8B writes
  longer, more elaborate code with more invented names. The 4B's errors are
  almost all replies the token budget cut off mid-code (16 of 22 in Stage~1).

  \item \textbf{Neither model uses the probe run, and the six percent in the
  probe-rate column is not probing.} 12 and 11 first replies of 192 are
  counted as probe code, every one of them cut off by the 1000-token budget.
  Table~\ref{tab:first-replies} shows what they are: 11 of the 4B's twelve and
  10 of the 8B's eleven are controllers the budget cut mid-code. The runner
  finds no \texttt{def policy} in code it cannot parse, so it took each as
  probe code; the sandbox rejected the unfinished block, the model received
  the rejection as its probe output, and wrote the controller again. The 4B's
  remaining reply is a code block of comments that ran and printed nothing;
  the 8B's is probe code that was cut off and printed nothing. No probe
  returned a reading in either run, so the estimate-error column is empty and
  the Stage~2 ride ratios carry nothing a probe found. (Corrected on
  2026-11-25. This item first read the 23 replies as probe code that the
  budget kept from running; Section~\ref{sec:budget} lifts the budget and
  finds no probe.)

  \item \textbf{For the 4B, the two-turn protocol helps at inference only by
  shortening the reply.} Reward rises from $-84$ to $-66$ because cut-off
  replies fall from $17.7\%$ to $3.6\%$ (median reply 2\,999 characters in
  Stage~1, 2\,086 in Stage~2), while success falls from
  $27\%$ to $23\%$ and fast success to zero.

  \item \textbf{Where the samples succeed} (Table~\ref{tab:by-third}): the
  4B succeeds on about half the high-third batches and on one in twenty to
  thirty of the low third. It cools at a fixed moderate rate that high limits
  tolerate and low limits punish: 93 and 132 batches ruined, and a mean ride
  ratio of $0.75$ to $0.79$ that averages over-riding low limits with
  under-riding high ones. The 8B mostly times out (51 and 31 of 192): it
  cools too slowly or stops; its ride ratio is $0.30$ to $0.50$.

  \item \textbf{The superseded first round agrees within sampling noise}
  (4B $-85$ and $-53$, 8B $-209$ and $-195$; the provenance comments in the
  source of this document name that round), so the sandbox bug floored
  twelve samples but did not shape the picture.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{For the ladder.} The 4B base is the model to train: the 8B
gives no better start at twice the memory. ``Whether to probe'' has a frozen
baseline of zero: no first reply of the 4B is a probe that returned a
reading, at 1000 tokens per turn or at 4000 (Section~\ref{sec:budget}). The
token budget of the training stages is still to be chosen;
Section~\ref{sec:budget} holds the measurement the choice rests on.


\section{The token budget: the 4B at 4000 tokens per turn}
\label{sec:budget}

The runs above allow 1000 new tokens per turn, and that cut closed $17.7\%$
of the 4B's Stage~1 replies and every reply counted as a probe. To see what
the model writes when nothing cuts it, both 4B runs were repeated with 4000
tokens per turn and nothing else changed: the same 48 tasks, 4 samples per
task, sampling settings, brief and scoring code. They are a fresh draw, not a
re-score. Tables~\ref{tab:budget-comparison} to~\ref{tab:budget-by-third} set
them next to the 1000-token runs of the 4B; the run names carry the budget.

\subsection{Reading}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.5em]
  \item \textbf{With room to write it, the 4B still does not probe.} At 4000
  tokens one first reply of 192 is counted as probe code, and it is a complete
  controller with a syntax error, not cut off
  (Table~\ref{tab:first-replies}). Over both budgets, none of the 384 first
  replies of the 4B is probe code that ran and returned a reading. The budget
  was not what kept the model from probing.

  \item \textbf{What it does instead is write probe code into the same reply
  as the controller.} 9 of the 191 controllers at 4000 tokens mention
  \texttt{env.reset} or \texttt{env.step} (6 of 180 at 1000 tokens): 5 in a
  separate function defined next to \texttt{policy}, 2 inside
  \texttt{policy}, where \texttt{env} does not exist, and 2 in comments only.
  A reply that defines \texttt{policy} is the controller and ends the task,
  so none of this code meets the probe batch. The two such replies read in
  full both cool at the full rate until the shower and take the reading there
  as the limit, which is the right experiment; what is missing is the order
  of the protocol, the probe code alone first and the controller after its
  output has come back. One first reply at 1000 tokens, a block of comments,
  states the misreading: ``Since we don't have env in the final controller, we
  must write the probe code in the same block [\ldots] So we can write probe
  code first, then the policy.'' The 8B does the same far more often: 38 of
  its 181 controllers mention the probe environment, 31 of them in a separate
  function.

  \item \textbf{Without the cut the replies are no longer.} The median first
  reply is 788 tokens in Stage~1 and 522 in Stage~2
  (Table~\ref{tab:reply-tokens}), against 814 and 553 under the 1000-token
  cut. A budget of 1000 lets $84.4\%$ of the Stage~1 first replies and
  $92.2\%$ of the Stage~2 ones finish; 1500 lets $97.9\%$ and $99.0\%$
  finish; 2000 lets $99.0\%$ and all of them. The longest Stage~2 reply is
  1\,735 tokens; one Stage~1 reply ran to the 4000-token end. For scale, the
  hand-written probe code that passes Stage~0 is 345 tokens and its
  controller 291.

  \item \textbf{What the 1000-token cut costs the frozen baseline is the
  replies it cuts, and little else.} In Stage~1 the reward rises from $-84.3$
  to $-62.2$: the samples that did not run fall from 22 to 11, the 16 syntax
  errors of the cut-off replies to none
  (Table~\ref{tab:budget-errors}), and successes rise from 52 to 61 of 192.
  In Stage~2 it rises from $-65.7$ to $-58.6$ with 45 successes of 192 at
  both budgets. Fast success stays at or under $3.1\%$, and the four runs
  stay between 97 and 123 points below the cautious blind reference. The two
  budgets are separate draws of 192 samples, so a difference of a few samples
  between them is not a finding.

  \item \textbf{The two-turn brief does not beat the one-turn brief once the
  cut is gone.} At 4000 tokens Stage~2 scores $-58.6$ against Stage~1's
  $-62.2$, with fewer successes ($23.4\%$ against $31.8\%$), more ruined
  batches (142 against 104), and fewer timeouts and errors (3 and 2 against
  16 and 11). The gap of about 19 points at 1000 tokens shrinks to under 4,
  which agrees with the reading above that the two-turn protocol helped only
  by shortening the reply.

  \item \textbf{The pattern by third is the same at both budgets}
  (Table~\ref{tab:budget-by-third}): at 4000 tokens the Stage~1 controllers
  succeed on $65.6\%$ of the high-third batches and $6.2\%$ of the low-third
  ones.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{What this settles and what it leaves open.} The token budget is
not a confound of the probe rate: the frozen 4B's probe rate is zero at
either budget, and the six percent reported at 1000 tokens were cut-off
controllers. The probe rate as the runner computes it counts a controller
that does not parse as a probe; that is a property of the metric and of the
protocol (such a reply gets a second turn), and it is not changed here. Two
decisions stay open, and this document takes neither. The first is the
budget of the training stages: 1000 tokens cuts about one in six of the
frozen model's Stage~1 first replies and one in thirteen of its Stage~2
ones, 1500 cuts about one in fifty and one in a hundred, and the memory
cost of longer turns in training has not been measured. The second is what
to do about a model that never probes before training starts: the training
stages with a probe run have no probing first replies to learn from, and
the replies above point at the brief's description of the two turns, not at
the budget.

\section{Reproduce}
\sloppy
% commits and jobs: see the provenance block at the top of this file
The weights: \texttt{hf download Qwen/Qwen3-8B --local-dir
models/hf\_base/qwen3-8b} on the cluster's run node (the 4B base is at
\texttt{models/hf\_base/iter\_000}). Each run is one job:
\begin{scriptsize}
\begin{verbatim}
hpc submit lora4vr jobs/hpi/stage1.sbatch --job-name=stage1-8b \
    --export=ALL,LORA4VR_GIT_COMMIT=$(git rev-parse HEAD),MODEL_PATH=models/hf_base/qwen3-8b,N_SAMPLES=4
hpc submit lora4vr jobs/hpi/stage2.sbatch --job-name=stage2-8b \
    --export=ALL,LORA4VR_GIT_COMMIT=$(git rev-parse HEAD),MODEL_PATH=models/hf_base/qwen3-8b,N_SAMPLES=4
hpc pull lora4vr/results/stage2-8b_<jobid> docs/stage12/
uv run python scripts/frozen_render.py --out docs/stage12/tables \
    stage1-4b=docs/stage12/stage1-4b_<jobid> stage2-4b=docs/stage12/stage2-4b_<jobid> \
    stage1-8b=docs/stage12/stage1-8b_<jobid> stage2-8b=docs/stage12/stage2-8b_<jobid>
\end{verbatim}
\end{scriptsize}
and the same with \texttt{MODEL\_PATH=models/hf\_base/iter\_000} for the 4B
runs. The token-budget runs of Section~\ref{sec:budget} are the 4B jobs with
the budget passed through \texttt{EXTRA\_ARGS}, and their tables are
rendered with the model's tokenizer for the token counts:
\begin{scriptsize}
\begin{verbatim}
E=ALL,LORA4VR_GIT_COMMIT=$(git rev-parse HEAD),MODEL_PATH=models/hf_base/iter_000,N_SAMPLES=4
hpc submit lora4vr jobs/hpi/stage1.sbatch --job-name=stage1-4b-4000 --time=4:00:00 \
    --export="$E,EXTRA_ARGS=--max-tokens 4000"
hpc submit lora4vr jobs/hpi/stage2.sbatch --job-name=stage2-4b-4000 --time=4:00:00 \
    --export="$E,EXTRA_ARGS=--max-tokens 4000"
hpc pull lora4vr/results/stage2-4b-4000_<jobid> docs/stage12/
uv run python scripts/frozen_render.py --out docs/stage12/tables_budget --macro-prefix SFT \
    --tokenizer models/hf_base/iter_000/tokenizer.json \
    stage1-4b-1000=docs/stage12/stage1-4b_<jobid> stage2-4b-1000=docs/stage12/stage2-4b_<jobid> \
    stage1-4b-4000=docs/stage12/stage1-4b-4000_<jobid> stage2-4b-4000=docs/stage12/stage2-4b-4000_<jobid>
\end{verbatim}
\end{scriptsize} Each result directory holds the job log, \texttt{stage<N>\_summary.json}
with its provenance block and per-task rows, and
\texttt{stage<N>\_samples.jsonl} with every sample: the full transcript, the
probe code, the tool output, the controller and its outcome.
